Article Title: FBI warns of Europe-like freezer hacking attacks in US supermarkets: 6 things the agency wants these companies to do
Article Text:
FBI warning on freezer attacks

Read FBI cyber branch’s warning

The @FBI and our partners are seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world. These systems help keep food, medicine, and other products at safe temperatures and are widely used across critical infrastructure sectors.

Attackers are targeting electronic temperature and refrigeration controllers, particularly in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. In at least one recent incident, attackers targeted refrigeration components at three foreign blood service facilities.

While this attack was unsuccessful due to the proper alert mechanisms in place, security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage

Potential links to US military base incidents

6 things the FBI wants companies to do

Take controllers off the public internet

Put access behind a firewall

Change default passwords

Learn how vendors configure devices

Set safe temperature limits

Ensure alerts reach the right contacts

The FBI has warned American grocery stores and cold storage facilities to lock down their refrigeration systems, following a wave of cyberattacks in Europe where hackers remotely raised freezer temperatures and ruined store inventories. In a post on X (formerly Twitter) by the FBI Cyber Branch, the agency said it is tracking malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide. These electronic controllers are used across critical infrastructure to keep food, medicine and other temperature-sensitive goods safe.The warning comes just days after supermarkets in France, Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit by remote hackers who raised fridge and freezer temperatures, forcing stores to throw out spoiled food. Hackers also recently targeted refrigeration components at three foreign blood service facilities – an attack that failed only because proper alert systems were in place.Security experts and federal investigators are looking closely at whether similar attacks have already reached American soil. In August, a series of freezer malfunctions ruined food at six US military base commissaries.Those incidents are currently under investigation as a suspected hack. The Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office, the Defense Commissary Agency, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service – all operating under the US Department of Defense – are working with French law enforcement to determine if the military base malfunctions are connected to the European grocery store attacks.In an accompanying video message, Brett Leatherman, Assistant Director of the FBI Cyber Division, explained how attackers are breaking in.“These systems protect food and medicine across healthcare, food and agriculture, and other critical sectors here in the United States as well. Attackers are getting in through controllers that are unpatched, reachable from the internet, or still using the default passwords listed in the manufacturer’s manual,” Leatherman said, New York Post reported.Once inside, hackers can alter system settings, leading to spoiled inventory and damaged equipment. To prevent this, the FBI is urging organisations to take six specific steps:
Article Summary: Attackers are targeting electronic temperature and refrigeration controllers, particularly in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. Security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings. The warning comes just days after supermarkets in France, Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit by remote hackers.

Article Title: America's datacentre buildout is hurting Japanese giant Softbank, as the company reports $7 billion net loss; but remains optimist as CFO Yoshimitsu Goto sees much promise in …
Article Text:
America's datacentre buildout is hurting Japanese giant Softbank, as the company reports $7 billion net loss; but remains optimist as CFO Yoshimitsu Goto sees much promise in …

Softbank’s AI borrowing becomes a concern for investors

Softbank has reported a $7 billion quarterly loss because of hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US and increases in financing payments, reports Reuters. The Japanese investment giant raised $56.5 billion during the July-September quarter, its highest ever quarterly total as founder Masayoshi Son continues to invest aggressively in AI. The company said it logged a $3.7 billion loss due to advance payments for equipment in US data centre projects after plans changed. The company expects these losses to be offset by rebates for future purchases and said that it will be entitled to rebates of up to $2.1 billion on future purchases.However, Softbank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto remains optimistic stating that data centre projects, which include a large-scale development in Pike County, Ohio, hold much promise.“These data centre projects have only just begun, and we expect that over the next five or 10 years, they will grow further and become much larger in scale,” he ​told a press briefing as stated in the report.As mentioned above, Softbank reported a quarterly loss of 1.1 trillion yen ($7 billion) far exceeding analysts' forecasts and ​comparing with a 2.5 trillion yen profit in the same period a year earlier. The quarterly results, as the report says, is expected to intensify questions about how well SoftBank will weather setbacks currently buffeting the AI sector.Softbank has invested heavily in AI – spanning from data centres to robotics as well as the $64.6 billion ⁠purchase of a 13% stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI . However, the company’s high AI borrowing has become a concern for some investors as its financing costs jumped to 462 billion yen in the quarter.
Article Summary: Softbank has reported a $7 billion quarterly loss because of hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US. The Japanese investment giant raised $56.5 billion during the July-September quarter, its highest ever quarterly total. The company said it logged a $3.7 billion loss due to advance payments for equipment in US data centre projects.

Article Title: Meta’s chief strategy officer Dave Wehner is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup; sends 'right mission' message; says: I have become increasingly ...
Article Text:
From Meta veteran to AI challenger

Fireworks eyes its next phase of growth

AI boom draws senior executives

AI race intensifies

Read Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner’s complete post here

Wehner's move underscores the growing pull of the AI industry as startups compete with larger rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and major cloud providers.

With fresh capital, rising valuations and growing enterprise demand for AI infrastructure, companies like Fireworks are increasingly attracting experienced leaders who see artificial intelligence as the next major technology platform.

Read Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner’s complete post here

I announced earlier this week that I am leaving Meta. I am deeply grateful to Mark Zuckerberg for showing what a truly founder-led company can achieve.

I am incredibly optimistic for Meta’s future.

At Meta, I was able to witness the most exciting opportunities in enterprise AI. That’s why today, I’m announcing that I will be joining Fireworks as CFO. I am thrilled to be joining a founder-led growth company where I can roll up my sleeves and put my experience to work.

Fireworks has the right mission for the moment. Companies will use AI to build on what makes them distinctive: their data and expertise.

Specialized intelligence gives them a way to capture those advantages and own their “alpha.” Open models offer price points that allow the technology to have the greatest impact. Fireworks is building the platform to make all of this possible.

I’ve known and respected Lin

for a long time. As I’ve spent more time with her and the people at Fireworks, I’ve become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There’s a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need.

I see AI as the most consequential technology shift of my lifetime. I’m excited to get to work and help build a business at the center of it.

Dave Wehner, Meta’s chief strategy officer and former chief financial officer, is leaving the social media giant to join fast-growing AI startup Lin Qiao-led Fireworks as its new CFO, marking another high-profile move from Big Tech into the artificial intelligence sector. Wehner announced the move in a post on X, saying he had become increasingly convinced of the opportunity ahead for the four-year-old startup. “Fireworks has the right mission for the moment,” he wrote. “I’ve become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There’s a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need.” Fireworks, which provides AI inference and model-training services built around open-source AI models, was valued at $17.5 billion in a Series D funding round in July.Wehner joined Meta, then known as Facebook, in 2012 and served as the company’s chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022 before taking on the role of chief strategy officer. During his tenure, he helped steer the company through a period of rapid growth, expanding advertising revenues and major bets on new technologies. In a statement to CNBC, Meta COO Javier Olivan praised Wehner's contributions, saying he helped guide the company through “tremendous growth and complexity” over the past 14 years while bringing disciplined thinking to some of its most important strategic decisions.At Fireworks, Wehner will oversee the company's finances and operations as it looks to scale further in the increasingly competitive AI market. CEO Lin Qiao said Wehner's experience would help the company as it enters its next stage of expansion.Founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, Fireworks allows developers and businesses to customise, train and run open AI models. The company counts investors such as Nvidia and Sequoia Capital among its backers and has reportedly held early discussions for another funding round that could value the startup between $30 billion and $40 billion.“Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again,” Qiao wrote in a LinkedIn post. “He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next.”Wehner's departure comes as venture-backed AI companies continue to attract seasoned executives from some of the world's largest technology firms. While Fireworks remains significantly smaller than Meta, which had a market capitalisation of about $1.56 trillion at Friday's close, the startup is positioning itself as a key player in the market for open AI models.The company has also faced challenges associated with rapid growth. In October, Fireworks disclosed a security incident involving unauthorised use of internal credentials that allowed limited access to environment variables used in evaluation jobs within a small number of customer accounts. The company said its investigation found no evidence of unauthorised access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information or inference traffic.Wehner's move underscores the growing pull of the AI industry as startups compete with larger rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and major cloud providers. With fresh capital, rising valuations and growing enterprise demand for AI infrastructure, companies like Fireworks are increasingly attracting experienced leaders who see artificial intelligence as the next major technology platform.
Article Summary: Dave Wehner, Meta’s chief strategy officer and former chief financial officer, is leaving the social media giant to join fast-growing AI startup Fireworks. Wehner announced the move in a post on X, saying he had become increasingly convinced of the opportunity ahead for the four-year-old startup. Fireworks provides AI inference and model-training services built around open-source AI models.

Article Title: Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide
Article Text:
Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide

How Meta’s AI technology identifies teen users

Parents in the US will receive Instagram notifications

Meta begins using Apple’s age-range signal in Australia

Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. As announced by the company, starting this month, parents in the United States will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections, and how they can help make sure their teen’s age is accurate. Meta said that the move will bring millions more teens worldwide under Instagram’s Teen Account safeguards. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide.Meta said it uses AI to find accounts that it suspects belong to teenagers, even when users have misrepresented their age. Once identified, these accounts are placed in Teen Account protections. These safeguards automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they can see and the amount of time they spend on the platform. Teen Accounts are available across Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.Meta said it has been using the technology to place more teens into age-appropriate experiences and is now expanding it globally based on the results so far.The company is also continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook.It plans to begin launching similar age-estimation technology globally on Threads later this year.Meta is also introducing a new way to inform parents about its age-assurance measures. Starting this month, parents in the United States will begin seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining how the platform determines whether teens are receiving age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article outlining Meta’s approach and how parents can help ensure their children have provided the correct age.The article, written by internet safety advocate Larry Magid, will be available to parents worldwide.Meta said its approach involves multiple layers, including efforts to keep children under 13 off its platforms, provide age-appropriate experiences for teenagers and help parents understand how they can support accurate age information.In Australia, Meta has started using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional way to determine a user’s age. Under the process, parents setting up a smartphone for their teen can choose to have the app store confirm the user’s age range. When the teen downloads an app, Apple can share that age-range signal with the developer, helping the app determine whether the user meets its age requirements.Meta said it is voluntarily using the signal. However, it argued that protections could remain inconsistent across apps as long as app stores and developers are not required to participate.The company has supported legislation that would require age verification and parental consent at the app-store level. Meta said a single verified age signal shared consistently with apps could be more effective and privacy-preserving than requiring every platform to conduct its own age checks.
Article Summary: Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide. Starting this month, parents in the US will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections.

Article Title: Anthropic unveils faster, cheaper Claude AI models as it gears up for mega IPO
Article Text:
Anthropic takes on OpenAI with faster, cheaper Claude AI models ahead of planned IPO

Anthropic on Monday unveiled two new artificial intelligence models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, as the OpenAI rival looks to strengthen its position in the rapidly expanding AI market ahead of its planned initial public offering (IPO).The company said the new models generate outputs up to 30 per cent faster than their Claude 5.1 predecessors and offer clearer communication with users. They will also be priced lower than previous Fable and Mythos releases, at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.Claude Fable 5.2 is designed for coding, reasoning and AI agent tasks, while Claude Mythos 5.2 is aimed at approved cybersecurity and life-sciences research applications.Anthropic said access to Mythos 5.2 would be restricted to organisations approved through its verification programmes for cybersecurity and life-sciences research. Fable 5.2, meanwhile, will be available more widely.The launch follows the company's rollout of Claude Haiku 5.5 in October as it continues to expand its AI product portfolio ahead of its planned IPO.The latest release comes amid intensifying competition in the AI industry, with OpenAI, Alphabet's Google and Meta Platforms rapidly introducing new models focused on coding, reasoning and AI agents to attract developers and enterprise customers.
Article Summary: Claude Fable 5.2 is designed for coding, reasoning and AI agent tasks, while Claude Mythos 5. 2 is aimed at approved cybersecurity and life-sciences research applications. The company said the new models generate outputs up to 30 per cent faster than their Claude 5.1 predecessors and offer clearer communication with users.

Article Title: Meta: Days before he got an offer from Meta, to lead the company's AI lab, Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a 'long note' whose first principle was that he does not need a lot of people, as what mat
Article Text:
Cheeky Pint

A 44-minute call that led to a major hire

Why Mark Zuckerberg chose Alexandr Wang

A ‘supernova’ recruiting push

The results and the stakes

Days before accepting an offer to lead Meta’s artificial intelligence efforts, Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a lengthy memo outlining how he would approach the company’s AI ambitions. According to a Fortune report, the first principle in that note was simple: success in AI is not about having the largest workforce, but about having the highest concentration of top talent. Wang, the 29-year-old co-founder of Scale AI who now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs, revealed details of the memo during an appearance alongside Zuckerberg on thepodcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison. The discussion offered a rare glimpse into the conversations that preceded one of the biggest executive hires in the AI industry.The partnership began taking shape in April 2025, shortly after Meta’s Llama 4 models received a lukewarm response. Wang recalled receiving a WhatsApp message from Zuckerberg asking whether he had time for a call. That conversation lasted about 44 minutes.Two days later, Wang sent Zuckerberg a detailed memo describing what he would do if he were running Meta’s AI division. Recalling the advice, Zuckerberg said the very first principle centred on “talent density.”“The very first thing is that you don’t need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters,” Zuckerberg said. According to the Meta CEO, the second principle was being willing to rebuild from scratch. Zuckerberg acknowledged that the company was unhappy with the direction of Llama 4 and was prepared to reorganise its AI efforts if necessary.The decision to put Wang in charge of Meta’s AI ambitions surprised some observers because the entrepreneur had built Scale AI into a data-labelling giant but had never personally led the training of a frontier AI model. Zuckerberg, however, said he had admired Wang for years and viewed him as one of the sharpest entrepreneurs of his generation. Before making the decision, he spoke with leaders across major AI research labs but remained convinced that Wang was the right person for the role. “I talked to like all the leaders of all the labs, like all the heads of research,” Zuckerberg said on the podcast. “And I was like, no, Alex is the guy.”Zuckerberg described what followed as a “supernova” recruiting effort. Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI to bring Wang aboard and reportedly offered $100 million pay packages to OpenAI researchers. Zuckerberg cleared his calendar for two months, and he said neither of them slept much in the first couple of months. Meta’s core research team in the lab has fewer than 200 people, and Wang said it is closer to 100. It is backed by larger infrastructure and product teams at a company of about 75,000 employees. Wang said he built a culture of “insecure overachievers.”The lab’s first model, Muse Spark, arrived in April. On Monday, Meta released Muse Wonder, the first model from the lab it calls frontier-class. Wang said it is state-of-the-art on his team’s measurements for personal and professional agent tasks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the flagship version lands roughly level with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic but a couple of points behind the leader, according to AI Weekly.The Muse app launched in the US on September 8 and quickly became the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store. It topped 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN. Zuckerberg said late last year that Meta was discussing spending as much as $100 billion or $200 billion, and recalled asking Wang whether he was sure it would work. Wang said Meta CFO Susan Li pulled him aside at an executive gathering in Hawaii to stress that the model has to work, because failure would be very bad in financial terms. Meta expects 2026 capital spending of $130 billion to $145 billion, nearly double last year’s $72.2 billion.Wang also praised Zuckerberg’s leadership, saying he has fully internalised power laws. Once Zuckerberg adopts a belief, Wang said, the speed and scale at which he will change earlier decisions are unusual.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, 29, is the co-founder of Scale AI and now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs. Mark Zuckerberg called Wang on WhatsApp and asked if he had time for a call. Two days later, Wang sent Zuckerberg a detailed memo describing what he would do if he were running Meta’s AI division. Zuckerberg described what followed as a ‘supernova’ recruiting effort.

Article Title: Chinese AI lab that Dario Amodei complained to the US government is targeting Nvidia' most-powerful chips that are banned in China; and the route the company is taking is Europe
Article Text:
Nvidia

Moonshot AI’s ‘European workaround’

AI companies racing to meet surging demand

Moonshot AI, the Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) lab previously accused by the White House of remotely tapping into advanced Nvidia chips in East Asia, has been looking to secure access to those same restricted processors through European data centers, CNBC has reported. Citing four people familiar with the private discussions, the report said that talks have taken place this year for Moonshot to rent computing capacity from “neoclouds” hosting Nvidia GPUs inside European facilities. Moonshot is the maker of the Kimi AI assistant and in September, the company was accused by Anthropic of unauthorised model distillation and terms-of-service violations by secretly routing user requests through Claude.CNBC reports that Moonshot has been trying to lease capacity powered by Nvidia’s Blackwell systems, the cutting-edge chips that are effectively barred from being imported into China under US export controls. While US export rules block the physical shipment of Nvidia’s most advanced hardware to China, renting them remotely through overseas data centers remains a legal gray area. Current US law does not give regulators broad authority to stop foreign companies from accessing restricted chips via cloud services hosted abroad.To get around the bottleneck in Europe, a Chinese AI firm typically leases capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that is legally allowed to buy the chips.Two sources told the publication that Moonshot was looking to rent European clusters for inference while one source noted the lab was also interested in clusters for model training. Discussions have included deals for Moonshot to access clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in the region. One source described the lab as “very aggressive” in its hunt for computing power, adding that talks in Europe have continued even after the White House accused Moonshot in July of accessing Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand.Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China’s premier model builders, known for its Kimi family of AI models. In July, the company released a new model that it claimed closed the performance gap with leading systems from US rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.Lower costs and improved capabilities have fueled a surge in global adoption for Chinese AI models throughout 2026. Around the launch of Kimi K3, demand grew so intense that Moonshot temporarily paused new subscriptions to protect computing power for existing users.“We’re adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches,” the company wrote in a LinkedIn post at the time.Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported last week that Nvidia has instructed cloud providers selling access to its chips that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese customers. Responding to those reports, an Nvidia spokesperson said: “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well. ”
Article Summary: Moonshot AI has been looking to secure access to restricted processors through European data centers, CNBC has reported. Talks have taken place this year for Moonshot to rent computing capacity from “neoclouds” hosting Nvidia GPUs inside European facilities.

Article Title: Months before Marco Rubio's memo to the US government, how an year-old report 'warned' America on Alice Huang and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as it called 'mystery lady CEO and billions in sales' to ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang with Alice Huang

What Rubio’s memo reportedly said

How Megaspeed got the chips

Poll Vote & Share your view What action should Nvidia take in response to the allegations against Megaspeed? Increase transparency Conduct a thorough investigation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nvidia’s link to Singapore’s Megaspeed is getting awkward. Before US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman, the New York Times had already rung the warning bells. Months before Nvidia launched its own independent investigation, the publication reported that the American intelligence agencies already suspected that the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security and used her company to import banned Nvidia chips in mainland China. Megaspeed is the Singapore-based firm where Alice Huang is a senior executive, and the company has reportedly spent billions of dollars in Nvidia chip purchases.According to a report by The NYT, Rubio oversaw a highly classified memo that circulated among senior administration officials in May. It warned that Jensen Huang had built a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and senior executive at Megaspeed. The memo was based on intelligence gathered through electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. People briefed on the matter said the memo was shared with officials holding high-level security clearances ahead of Trump’s China trip in May.US officials suspected Megaspeed of illegally smuggling restricted Nvidia semiconductors into mainland China.However, an October 2025 report by the publication already red-flagged this, claiming that Commerce Department officials had been investigating whether Megaspeed – which has close ties to Chinese tech firms – is helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions. The report says more than a half dozen current and former officials and others familiar with the companies said so, on condition of anonymity, because the examination is not public.The earlier report had described a scene from a humid June night the year before. Jensen Huang was holding court with several of Nvidia’s major Asian customers at a bar with sweeping views of Taipei. They stood and toasted the booming AI industry. Next to him stood Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive. Her company was poised to buy $2 billion of Nvidia AI technology over the next year. She and Megaspeed were little-known players in the AI industry, but their link to Nvidia and its chief had become a preoccupation in Washington.Not just US but Singapore police were also investigating Megaspeed for breaching local laws. The inquiry raises questions about how closely Nvidia tracks where its AI chips end up. It also highlights how easily American export laws might be sidestepped.Megaspeed split off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023. It then set up a subsidiary in Malaysia that quickly bought nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia’s most advanced products. Citing records from the trade data platform ImportGenius, most of those chips came from the US branch of a Chinese company that has already been sanctioned for providing technology to the Chinese military.Megaspeed has sent those chips to data centres in Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to serve customers in China remotely. That is not necessarily illegal, but it can be unlawful if done on behalf of a Chinese company.Another report from The New York Times, published last month, claimed that when US officials told Trump about a Chinese spy plot, he took no action. Reason: the report explains that the US was already leading China in the AI race and Trump did not want to ‘disrupt’ Nvidia’s chip sales, which were helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.Notably, none of the spying claims have been proven, and Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe national security or its trade secrets were compromised.
Article Summary: US officials suspected Megaspeed of illegally smuggling restricted Nvidia semiconductors into mainland China. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman. The New York Times had already rung the warning bells months before Nvidia launched its own independent investigation.

Article Title: In December 2025, a report claimed that Megaspeed, whose CEO Jensen Huang has admitted having affair with, is facing investigation over smuggling Nvidia chips to China; here's the statement that Singa
Article Text:
Megaspeed denies illegal chip transfers

Company threatened legal action

Renewed attention after reports involving Nvidia CEO

Read Megaspeed's official statement here

We are aware of the recent article published by Bloomberg which has raised concerns regarding our operations.

We would like to clarify that the article contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers.

We want to be absolutely clear: over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and NVIDIA.

These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company.

We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.

Our company has always adhered to the law, and we take these accusations seriously. As such, we do not rule out pursuing legal action to protect our reputation and to hold Bloomberg accountable for the misleading nature of the article.

We appreciate the continued trust and support from our clients and partners.

Megaspeed December 23, 2025

Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed, which has recently come under renewed attention following reports about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with one of its executives, continues to stand by a statement it first issued nearly 10 months ago denying allegations that it was involved in illegally transferring Nvidia chips to China. The statement, dated December 23, 2025, was released after a Bloomberg report raised questions about Megaspeed's operations and suggested the company may have played a role in moving restricted AI chips into China. The company rejected the allegations, describing the report as containing "misleading information and incorrect insinuations."In its official response, Megaspeed said there was "no evidence" that it had violated export-control rules or engaged in illicit transfers of advanced semiconductors. The company said it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews over a six-month period by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, and Nvidia itself."These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said in the statement.Megaspeed added that it operates in compliance with all applicable export-control regulations and maintains "the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."The Singapore-based firm also signalled that it could pursue legal remedies over the reporting."Our company has always adhered to the law, and we take these accusations seriously. As such, we do not rule out pursuing legal action to protect our reputation and to hold Bloomberg accountable for the misleading nature of the article," the statement said. The company concluded by thanking customers and partners for their support.The New York Times reported on October 29 that US intelligence agencies believed Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and senior Megaspeed executive, was passing information to Beijing. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the report, surveillance of her as part of the chip-smuggling investigation revealed her close relationship with the Nvidia chief. The Commerce Department investigation, which began in late 2024, was later handed to the Justice Department, the Times reported. China’s embassy has called the allegations groundless smears.Nvidia opened an investigation into Jensen Huang on Sunday after he acknowledged to the company that he had been intimate with Alice Huang. The company said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Nvidia has said claims that Megaspeed diverted chips to China were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said Alice Huang was not investigated over alleged ties to China, though authorities there have confirmed a domestic investigation into Megaspeed over corporate fraud and supplier misrepresentation, according to WION.
Article Summary: Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed stands by statement it issued nearly 10 months ago denying allegations it was involved in illegally transferring Nvidia chips to China. The company said it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews over a six-month period by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security.

Article Title: As US President seeks support for American Affordability and Jobs Act; calls for support from senators and citizens; says: Will lower electricity costs and protect …
Article Text:
Donald Trump

Faster approvals for energy projects

What the bill is

Data centres would pay their own power costs

Growing concern over AI-driven electricity demand

China competition at centre of debate

US President Donald Trump has called on senators and American citizens to support the American Affordability and Jobs Act, arguing that the legislation would boost energy production, reduce electricity costs and ensure data centres bear the costs of the power infrastructure they require. In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump described the proposed legislation, identified as S. 5653, as a "BIG WIN" for US energy independence and energy dominance. He said the measure would speed up approvals for critical energy projects and codify what he called his "ratepayer protection pledge." "Call your Senators, and get them to support the American Affordability and Jobs Act," Trump wrote, urging public backing for the bill.Trump said the legislation includes permitting reforms that would allow pipelines, mines and power plants to be built more quickly, helping expand domestic energy production and infrastructure.According to the president, the measure is designed to lower electricity costs for consumers while supporting economic growth and job creation through faster project development. The proposal aligns with Trump's broader energy agenda since returning to the White House, which has focused on expanding fossil fuel production and easing regulatory barriers.Earlier this year, he declared a national energy emergency and renewed his "drill, baby, drill" push aimed at increasing domestic energy output.The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 was introduced on September 30 by a bipartisan group of senators including Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee and Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich. The 417-page bill would change federal permitting procedures, including environmental reviews. According to a summary reported by trade outlet Contractor, it would speed federal approvals for energy and infrastructure projects and require large data centres, defined there as those with 20 megawatts or more of demand, to cover the full cost of grid infrastructure they require, so residential and commercial ratepayers don’t absorb it. Supporters, including the National Association of Counties, say it would modernise an outdated permitting system.Some environmental and public-interest groups oppose the bill. Public Citizen and campaigners for public lands argue that it weakens protections and favours fast-tracked data centres. Critics have also objected to the bill being negotiated mainly behind closed doors, and have raised concerns that it could give the administration wide leeway on permits. Supporters say the bill contains safeguards. No Senate vote has been reported yet.A key feature of the bill is its approach to rapidly growing electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centres. Trump said the legislation would require data centres to pay for their own electricity infrastructure rather than passing those costs on to households and other consumers. He also said data centre operators would be required to invest in surrounding communities. The president warned that excessive restrictions on energy and data centre development in the United States could benefit China, arguing that projects rejected domestically may simply move overseas.The issue of how to manage surging electricity demand from AI infrastructure has become a bipartisan concern in Washington.The House recently passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. According to a Department of Energy-backed report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, data centres accounted for 4.4% of US electricity consumption in 2023, with that figure projected to rise to as much as 12% by 2028.The Congressional Budget Office has said the legislation would apply to non-residential data centres with peak electricity demand of at least 100 megawatts at a single facility, while allowing states to decide whether to adopt the proposed federal standards.Concerns over maintaining US leadership in artificial intelligence have increasingly become part of the discussion around data centre expansion. Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein recently warned that opposition to data centre projects could become "a gift to China." Meanwhile, technology analyst Dan Ives has argued that a Democratic takeover of Congress could slow the buildout of AI infrastructure by jeopardising some planned US data centre projects.Trump echoed similar concerns in his appeal for support, framing the American Affordability and Jobs Act as both an energy and economic competitiveness measure aimed at ensuring the United States remains ahead in the global AI race while shielding consumers from rising electricity costs.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has called on senators and American citizens to support the American Affordability and Jobs Act. He said the measure would speed up approvals for critical energy projects and codify what he called his "ratepayer protection pledge" A key feature of the bill is its approach to rapidly growing electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centres.

Article Title: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian says he wants his daughter to use AI every day; reveals how she changed his understanding of the technology
Article Text:
Alexis Ohanian wants his daughter to explore big questions with AI

Alexis Ohanian says his daughter changed how he thinks about speaking to AI

AI is becoming part of her drawing sessions

Alexis Ohanian's vision for raising a daughter who can use AI as a creative superpower

Parenthood has influenced the way he thinks about technology

Alexis Ohanian has spent much of his career building and investing in technology, but one of his most useful lessons about artificial intelligence has come from watching his seven-year-old daughter use it. The Reddit co-founder says he wants Olympia to work with AI every day, treating it as a tool for asking questions, exploring ideas and developing her creativity. Their conversations at the dinner table have become part of that routine. Yet it is not simply what she asks about an AI system that has caught his attention. Watching her speak naturally to the technology has also made him reconsider assumptions he had carried from years of using computers.During an interview on the Possible podcast, hosted by Reid Hoffman and Aria Finger, Ohanian described a family routine built around asking a big question over dinner. It began before AI became part of the household. When his daughter was younger, he would try to answer her questions himself, looking things up when he did not know enough.“Even just seeing my own seven-year-old’s relationship to AI—and the ChatGPT app is definitely the one that runs all the numbers for us—and seeing the way she converses with it.Seeing the way we do a big question every night at dinner. And we started doing this pre-AI, and so poor papa had to be the answer, and we’d look it up if I didn’t know, but she was also younger, so the questions were a lot easier back then. But now the questions are getting harder. ”He sees this as a change in the way children can approach information. Previous generations had reference books and dictionaries, followed by search engines such as Google. For Olympia, conversational AI is becoming another way to find answers, but one that allows her to continue asking questions rather than stopping at a list of search results.Ohanian said he wants her to use the technology every day. His aim is not to make AI a replacement for learning, but to let her become comfortable using it while she develops her own interests and abilities.One of the more personal observations Ohanian shared concerned the way Olympia communicates with ChatGPT. He had spent years getting used to typing questions into computers and had little reason to reconsider that habit. His daughter approached the technology differently.For a child who has grown up with much better speech-recognition tools, speaking to an AI assistant can feel more natural than typing. Ohanian said watching her converse with the system helped him recognise that his own preference for typing was shaped by older experiences with speech-to-text software, which had often been unreliable.He recalled, “I think because I was so hung up with speech-to-text being bad for so much of my life, that it took a seven-year-old—who’s really only known amazing speech-to-text—to help me realize like, “My God, you’re right. This paradigm is here.” And this is the fun part.”Ohanian also described how he and Olympia have been experimenting with AI as part of their creative activities. He recently found some of his childhood sketchbooks, which his parents had kept, and photographed several of the drawings. Using a recent version of ChatGPT, he showed his daughter how those pencil sketches could be turned into coloured illustrations.Some of the drawings were unfinished. That did not prevent them from being transformed into more complete images, giving Olympia a chance to see how an early idea could develop into something different.The process has also become part of their drawing sessions. Ohanian said they follow tutorials from the YouTube channel Art for Kids, drawing alongside the instructor with physical markers and paper. Once they have finished, he can photograph their work and use AI tools to alter or extend the images. They can see a drawing brought to life, including imagined versions of it moving through space.For Ohanian, the technology adds possibilities to an existing activity rather than taking its place. The child remains involved in the creative work, while the software provides a way to see the result differently.Ohanian's enthusiasm for AI does not mean he wants his daughter to skip traditional learning. He specifically said that reading, writing and arithmetic remain fundamentals she needs to understand.He has also introduced Olympia to Synthesis Tutor to support her maths homework. He described it as part of the family's efforts to use available tools to help with learning, rather than relying on AI for every task.His wider point is that children will need to know how to make use of increasingly capable systems. He described AI as a kind of superpower that he wants Olympia to have, particularly when it comes to creativity and turning ideas into something tangible.In the interview, he suggested that the value of these tools would increasingly depend on what people chose to do with them. He spoke about agency, persistence and creativity as qualities that would remain important even as AI systems became more capable.Ohanian's comments about Olympia fit into a wider discussion about how technology should affect people's lives. He has spoken about wanting to build products and support companies that reflect the kind of world he hopes his daughters will grow up in.That thinking was part of the reason he established his venture firm, Seven Seven Six, in 2020. In the podcast interview, he explained that becoming a father had made him think more carefully about the professional decisions he was making and the values those decisions represented. He wanted to be able to explain his work to his daughter as she grew older and show her that he had tried to build businesses he could be proud of.His interest in AI also extends beyond family life. He discussed how the technology could help online communities, including by taking some of the repetitive work away from volunteer moderators. He believes AI agents could handle tasks such as identifying spam, leaving community leaders with more time for activities that involve organising people and building relationships.He also spoke about possible uses in sport, where AI could help with player development, scouting and safety, particularly in areas such as women's sport that have historically received less investment.
Article Summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian wants his daughter to explore big questions with AI. He says he wants Olympia to work with AI every day, treating it as a tool for asking questions, exploring ideas and developing her creativity. Ohanian said watching her converse with the system helped him recognise that his own preference for typing was shaped by older experiences with speech-to-text.

Article Title: Law professor shares 'public service announcement' on Claude AI Agent after it deletes his lecture notes of an entire year and current syllabus; chatbot said in apology: I deleted your Fall 2026 …
Article Text:
AI Agent (Representative photo)

AI agent deletes file and says, ‘You’re right to be angry’

Growing list of AI Agent mishaps

A University of Chicago law professor is warning others about the risks of handing everyday tasks over to artificial intelligence (AI) agents after Claude AI accidentally wiped out his current syllabus and a full year of Constitutional Law lecture notes. William Baude, the Harry Kalven, Jr. Professor of Law and Faculty Director of the Constitutional Law Institute at the University of Chicago Law School, shared the experience as a public service announcement. Fortunately, the files were later recovered through Dropbox, but the incident serves as the latest cautionary tale as AI tools become more common.Baude had given Claude (unclear which specific model) what seemed like a simple, routine job: updating the page numbers in an old set of lecture notes. Things went wrong fast. When Baude came back from his lunch break, he was greeted by a message from the chatbot.“I deleted your Fall 2026 FINAL syllabus .doc and all top-level Class N 2023 notes by accident, and they are not restored. The page check found one wrong cite... but I haven’t edited the notes,” Claude wrote. After delivering the bad news, the AI politely asked if Baude could restore the missing documents from Dropbox, or if he wanted it to try again from the browser pane.Baude’s response was blunt: “WTF!!!!.”The chatbot was quick to take the blame, offering an apologetic reply. “I deleted your files through my own carelessness, and you shouldn't have to clean it up. You're right to be angry,” it confessed, adding, “I'm trying the Dropbox restore page again now, and I won't click Restore or change anything without telling you first.”While Baude got his work back, the close call highlights an obvious rule for anyone letting AI tinker with their folders: always keep backups of important files. What makes his case stand out is that the AI appeared to erase the documents purely by accident, rather than acting on its own accord.As concerning as it is for an AI tool to make a mistake of this scale, Baude’s close call isn't an isolated event. Several other high-profile blunders have surfaced in recent months.In October, an AI agent reportedly deleted an entire television show’s edit just weeks before its scheduled release, leaving the show unable to air.In April, a Claude agent deleted an entire company database in just nine seconds, unprompted, after hitting a roadblock and deciding that deleting a Railway volume was the only way forward.In another instance, Claude accidentally wiped out a developer’s entire profile directory while trying to back up those very files, later blaming the mistake on a typo.
Article Summary: University of Chicago law professor warns others about risks of handing everyday tasks over to artificial intelligence. Claude AI accidentally wiped out his current syllabus and a full year of Constitutional Law lecture notes. Fortunately, the files were later recovered through Dropbox, but the incident serves as the latest cautionary tale as AI tools become more common.

Article Title: Six-month-old memo that first warned US government about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair
Article Text:
Huang acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not provide details about the relationship.

What the memo reportedly said

Jensen Huang’s apology and the Nvidia probe

Questions over China trip participation

Surveillance allegedly identified Nvidia chief

Megaspeed under scrutiny

A highly classified memo drafted under the supervision of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior Trump administration officials months ago that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was involved in a close relationship with a woman whom US intelligence agencies believed was working for China's top spy service, according to a report by The New York Times. The report says the memo, circulated this spring ahead of President Donald Trump's China trip in May, was based on classified intelligence gathered through electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and senior executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed. US officials reportedly concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security and was in a close relationship with Jensen Huang, despite the two sharing no family connection.According to The New York Times, Rubio personally oversaw the drafting of the memo, which was distributed to administration officials holding high-level security clearances. The existence of the memo highlights that concerns about the relationship had reached the highest levels of the US government months before the matter became public. The report notes that the warning circulated even as Jensen Huang remained one of the most influential voices shaping Trump's approach to artificial intelligence policy.Huang has repeatedly argued against broader restrictions on AI chip exports and has advocated allowing sales of most Nvidia technology to China, with the exception of the company's newest products. The State Department and White House declined to comment, the newspaper reported.In a message to employees, Huang wrote: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” The Times reported that he acknowledged being intimate with Alice Huang. Other outlets, citing Bloomberg, say his message did not name the other person, so attribute that point carefully. Nvidia said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will oversee the investigation. It added that it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Nvidia has said Huang’s contacts with her were consistent with meetings he has with the company’s many customers and that customers like Megaspeed do not receive classified business information. The company says Huang supports the investigation.The report further claims that Jensen Huang was initially left off the list of business and technology executives invited to accompany Trump on his May visit to China. While it remains unclear whether the exclusion was linked to the classified memo, administration officials reportedly had concerns about Huang's influence on White House AI policy. However, after reports surfaced about his absence from the delegation, Trump personally invited Huang to join the trip, asking him to meet Air Force One during a stop in Alaska. The New York Times reported that Trump later praised Huang publicly, describing it as an honour to have "the Great Jensen Huang" travelling with the delegation to China.The newspaper had previously reported that Trump was briefed about intelligence surveillance involving Alice Huang roughly a year earlier. The surveillance reportedly revealed a close relationship between the Chinese executive and an unnamed US citizen. After officials requested that the American's identity be unmasked, the individual was identified as Jensen Huang.According to the report, Trump chose not to act at the time, partly because Nvidia's leadership position in AI is considered strategically important to US competition with China and because the company's success has been viewed as beneficial to financial markets.At the centre of the allegations is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has purchased billions of dollars worth of Nvidia AI chips in recent years. US officials reportedly suspect the company has helped move restricted advanced chips into China, bypassing export controls.The report states that despite maintaining a limited physical presence, Megaspeed purchased about $2 billion worth of Nvidia products and built Southeast Asian data centres that provide computing services to Chinese technology giant Alibaba.Nvidia has said Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were consistent with meetings he routinely has with customers and industry executives. The company has also maintained that customers such as Megaspeed do not receive classified Nvidia information. Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment, according to The New York Times.
Article Summary: Report: A classified memo warned that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was involved in a close relationship with a woman whom US intelligence agencies believed was working for China's top spy service. The memo was based on classified intelligence gathered through electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and senior executive at Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed. US officials reportedly concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Huang has acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not provide details about the relationship.

Article Title: Florida's new property tax cuts that 'proved' Google co-founder Larry Page, Oracle founder Larry Ellison, Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and other billionaires move to ‘Billionaire Bunkers’ may be right; als
Article Text:
Google co-founder Larry Page

What is Florida’s new property tax rule

Why Florida’s property tax cuts are raising concerns

Florida’s new property tax cuts are offering another financial incentive to wealthy homeowners buying luxury properties in the state, including billionaires such as Google co-founder Larry Page , Oracle founder Larry Ellison, Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who have invested heavily in South Florida real estate. However, the same tax overhaul that could benefit property owners has triggered a growing debate over whether smaller towns may lose funding for essential public services, including police, firefighters and emergency medical services. A Fortune report has warned that the changes could push some rural communities towards what a former Republican lawmaker described as “rural dark ages”.Florida voters approved Amendment 3 in the November 2026 election, expanding the state’s homestead exemption for non-school property taxes. The exemption will increase from the current $51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and rise further to $250,000 in 2028.The measure also reduces the annual cap on taxable value increases for rental and commercial properties from 10% to 5%. While the higher homestead exemption is primarily aimed at providing relief to residents facing rising living costs, the lower assessment cap could also benefit owners of secondary properties and commercial assets.For billionaires who own multiple luxury estates, investment properties and commercial holdings in Florida, the reduced assessment cap could slow the growth of their property tax bills. However, the flat-dollar homestead exemption itself offers relatively little savings on properties worth tens or hundreds of millions of dollars.In the earlier story, real estate attorney Raul Gastesi estimated that a fully phased-in exemption could save a typical homeowner roughly $2,085 annually at the statewide average non-school tax rate. For a $50 million luxury estate, the annual tax bill would fall only slightly, from approximately $524,000 to $522,000.While the changes could reduce property tax bills, local governments are expected to face significant revenue losses. State economists have projected that local governments could lose nearly $5 billion in the first year and almost $12 billion annually once the exemption is fully implemented.According to Fortune, Amendment 3 requires remaining tax revenue to be spent on public safety and other local services. However, it does not mandate that police, fire and emergency medical services receive funding first or guarantee them a minimum level of financial support.This has raised concerns among sheriffs, police chiefs, fire chiefs and local government officials, who have warned that the tax cuts could force them to reduce staffing and services.Former Republican state senator Jeff Brandes, who leads the Florida Policy Project, has argued that smaller and rural communities could face the greatest pressure because they have fewer alternative sources of revenue than larger cities such as Miami.“The amendment itself sends no reimbursement to fiscally constrained counties, the poorest and most rural places with the least room to absorb a loss, and nothing in the amendment guarantees that police and fire will be protected,” Brandes said.He warned that the effects could gradually weaken local communities.“That is how rural Florida slides into rural dark ages: slower emergency response, crumbling roads, shorter library hours, shuttered recreation programs. Fewer services discourage investment. Less investment thins the tax base. A thinner tax base means fewer services. The dark ages won’t arrive all at once. They’ll arrive one closed fire station at a time.”The concerns extend beyond local government budgets. Reduced funding for fire departments could potentially affect fire protection ratings used by insurance companies to assess risk. An Insurance Information Institute spokesman told Bloomberg: “A reduction in fire protection services in a community can lead to a lower ISO rating,”The spokesman added: “The ISO rating is among numerous risk factors property insurers use to underwrite homes in Florida and could potentially cause premiums to increase if the rating is downgraded.”
Article Summary: Florida voters approved Amendment 3 in the November 2026 election, expanding the state’s homestead exemption for non-school property taxes. Amendment 3 requires remaining tax revenue to be spent on public safety and other local services. However, it does not mandate that police, fire and emergency medical services receive funding first or guarantee them a minimum level of financial support.

Article Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he does not want his son to have an AI chatbot as his best friend; reveals why children need greater protection from AI
Article Text:
Why Sam Altman is cautious about introducing AI to his children

What Sam Altman said about AI becoming a child's best friend

Experts are concerned about children forming emotional bonds with AI

Nearly three in four teenagers have used AI companions, study finds

What UNICEF says about protecting children from AI companions

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. He made that particular remark during a US Senate hearing in May 2025. More recently, in an exclusive interview with Vanity Fair, published on October 5, 2026, Altman discussed raising children in a world increasingly shaped by AI and said he had not decided at what age he would allow his own children to use ChatGPT. He also voiced concerns about excessive technology use during childhood and the potential effects of emerging technologies on developing brains. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.Speaking to Vanity Fair, Altman said he had not settled on an appropriate age for his children to start using ChatGPT. He indicated that he was not comfortable introducing the technology to them at their current age.The OpenAI chief also expressed support for limiting children's exposure to technology more broadly.He believes young children should have opportunities to spend time outdoors, play in nature and experience the world beyond screens.Altman raised concerns about children becoming accustomed to touchscreens and short-form videos at an early age. He also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the effects of emerging technologies on developing brains.He acknowledged that children growing up today would inevitably encounter AI and would need to understand how to use it. However, he questioned whether introducing conversational AI during early childhood was necessary, particularly when its long-term effects on development are still being studied.Altman had addressed the question of AI companionship during a US Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation hearing on May 8, 2025.During the hearing, Senator Bernie Moreno referred to Altman's experience as a new father and asked whether he wanted his child's best friend to be an AI bot. Altman responded directly: "I do not."He subsequently explained that children needed a much higher level of protection when interacting with AI services than adult users. He said OpenAI wanted to give adults considerable freedom in using its products while applying stricter rules and safeguards for younger users.Altman also acknowledged the difficulty of reliably determining whether an online user is a child or an adult. He said that if technology companies could identify users' ages with greater certainty, they could offer adults more flexibility while maintaining tighter restrictions for children.During the same discussion, he raised concerns about people increasingly turning to AI systems for life advice and emotional support. He described the development as relatively new and said it needed to be understood and monitored carefully.The growing popularity of AI companion applications has prompted warnings from child welfare organisations and psychological experts. Unlike conventional search engines or digital assistants, AI companions are designed to maintain conversations, respond to personal information and simulate relationships.This can make interactions feel like conversations with friends, mentors or confidants. However, the responses are generated by AI systems rather than people with genuine emotions or personal experiences.In June 2025, the American Psychological Association (APA) published its health advisory, Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being. It highlighted concerns about adolescents developing unhealthy relationships with chatbots and warned that young users may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intentions of information provided by AI systems.The advisory also warned that adolescents may struggle to distinguish simulated empathy from genuine human understanding. Strong attachments to AI characters could interfere with the development of real-world relationships and social skills.The APA recommended age-appropriate privacy settings, interaction limits, transparency about AI-generated responses and human oversight. It also called for developers to establish clear boundaries around simulated human relationships to prevent AI systems from undermining real-world connections.The organisation acknowledged that AI can support young people through educational and creative activities, including brainstorming, summarising and understanding information. However, it emphasised the need to make children aware of the technology's limitations.Research published by Common Sense Media on July 16, 2025, highlighted how widely AI companions had spread among teenagers in the United States.Its report, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, surveyed 1,060 US teenagers aged 13 to 17 in April and May 2025. It found that 72% had used AI companions, while 52% said they used them at least a few times a month. Around 33% reported using these platforms for social interaction and relationships.Among teenagers who had used AI companions, 33% said they had chosen to discuss important or serious matters with an AI companion instead of a real person. The survey also found that 24% of AI companion users had shared personal or private information, such as their real name, location or personal secrets, with these platforms.The research also offered a more nuanced picture of teenagers' relationships with AI. Despite widespread adoption, 80% of teenagers who had used AI companions said they spent more time with real-life friends than with AI companions. Additionally, 67% found conversations with AI less satisfying than conversations with their real-life friends.The findings suggest that although AI companions are becoming part of teenagers' social experiences, many young users continue to value human friendships more highly.UNICEF has also highlighted the risks associated with AI systems designed to act as friends or emotional companions.In a July 2025 article published by UNICEF Innocenti, titled The Risky New World of Tech's Friendliest Bots, researchers highlighted concerns about children's growing use of AI companions. The article featured research and an interview with digital innovation specialist Samia Firmino, examining the potential effects of these platforms on young users.It raised concerns about inadequate safety protections, inappropriate chatbot responses and the possibility of children developing unhealthy attachments to artificial companions.UNICEF subsequently updated its Guidance on AI and Children in December 2025. The third version included specific recommendations addressing AI companions and their potential impact on children's rights and well-being.The guidance calls on governments and technology companies to prioritise children's safety, protect their personal information, ensure transparency and establish accountability for AI systems. It also emphasises the importance of designing technology around children's developmental needs and preparing them to use AI responsibly.UNICEF recognises that AI can provide educational opportunities and improve accessibility for children, including those with disabilities. However, it stresses that these benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with children's interactions with increasingly sophisticated AI systems.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots. He said he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu warns of looming jobs crisis says, ‘problem is about to get worse’
Article Text:
Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu

China's growth story faces employment challenge

AI and automation putting pressure on white-collar jobs

Entrepreneurship must become the alternative

Read Sridhar Vembu’s complete post here

"For decades, young Chinese were promised a simple deal: Study hard. Get a good job. Become richer than your parents. That deal is breaking"

China is the factory of the world, has impressive technology capabilities across a vast array of sectors and runs a $1.2 trillion merchandise trade surplus and yet is not able to create jobs for a big cohort of her college-educated youth.

Approximately 70% of all unemployed individuals in the 20-to-24 age group hold university degrees in China.

Our modern educational and economic system around the world trains young people for "steady paycheck" jobs and those jobs are not just not growing, they are under serious challenge due to automation and AI.

This problem is about to get worse, not better.

What is the solution? Dramatic gains in entrepreneurship and self-employment. That has been the foundation of prosperity even in America all the way until the mid 20th century. The rise of the big industrial and corporate "steady paycheck" job is a relatively recent phenomenon. We have to move away from that model.

Policymakers in India must pay heed.

Zoho founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu has raised an alarm about the future of employment. Vembu argued that the traditional promise of education leading to secure, well-paying jobs is now breaking down, mainly in the face of automation and artificial intelligence. Reacting to a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) talking about the increasing youth unemployment in China, Vembu emphasised that the policymakers in India should take note of the challenges faced by the world’s second-largest economy. Vembu's comments came in response to a widely shared post that described China's youth employment situation as a potential generational challenge. The post claimed that unemployment among Chinese citizens aged 16-24 has reached 18%, while the rate for those aged 25-29 stands at 7.4%. It also highlighted a record 12.7 million college graduates entering the job market this year, alongside concerns that AI adoption could further reduce entry-level employment opportunities.In a post on X, Vembu cited China's economic strength, noting that the country remains "the factory of the world," possesses advanced technological capabilities across numerous sectors, and runs a merchandise trade surplus of roughly $1.2 trillion.Despite those strengths, he said China is struggling to generate enough jobs for a large section of its college-educated youth.According to Vembu, around 70% of unemployed individuals in China's 20-to-24 age group hold university degrees, highlighting a growing mismatch between educational outcomes and labour market opportunities.The Zoho founder argued that the issue extends beyond China and reflects a broader global challenge. He said modern education and economic systems have largely been designed to prepare young people for stable salaried employment, but those jobs are increasingly coming under pressure from automation and AI. "Our modern educational and economic system around the world trains young people for 'steady paycheck' jobs and those jobs are not just not growing, they are under serious challenge due to automation and AI," Vembu wrote. He added that the situation is likely to worsen rather than improve in the coming years.Vembu suggested that a dramatic increase in entrepreneurship and self-employment could be the answer. He pointed to the historical role of small businesses and self-employment in driving prosperity in the United States before the rise of large corporations and industrial employment."The rise of the big industrial and corporate 'steady paycheck' job is a relatively recent phenomenon. We have to move away from that model," he said.
Article Summary: Zoho founder and chief scientist Sridhar Vembu has raised an alarm about the future of employment. He argued that the traditional promise of education leading to secure, well-paying jobs is now breaking down, mainly in the face of automation and artificial intelligence. The Zoho founder suggested that a dramatic increase in entrepreneurship and self-employment could be the answer.

Article Title: As Jensen Huang's affair shocks global business world, five things Elon Musk agrees about Nvidia CEO
Article Text:
As Jensen Huang's affair shocks global business world, five things Elon Musk agrees about Nvidia CEO

Here’s what the X user wrote about Jensen Huang that Elon Musk agreed with

1) Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation

2) he did something incredibly dumb

3) it was bad for America

4) but my guess is there was no bad intention

5) two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership

Jensen Huang admits affair with Singapore-based company's CEO

Elon Musk has voiced agreement with an X post defending Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid controversy surrounding his affair, which has sent shockwaves through the global business world. X user Shaun Maguire listed five points about Jensen Huang, praising him as one of the greatest entrepreneurs of his generation while acknowledging that he made a serious mistake.
