Article Title: A plant grower posted photos of giant water lilies on Instagram; the pictures led researchers to first new giant waterlily species in 177 years; here's what makes them believe that there is 'trouble'
Article Text:
Representative Image

How Instagram photos prompted a search

Why researchers are concerned about its future

Giant waterlily photos shared on Instagram have led scientists to a new species. Pictures posted by US plant nursery owner Jeremiah Harris on the Meta-owned social media platform caught the attention of the UK’s Kew waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena, prompting a search through satellite imagery and an expedition to remote Colombian lakes. Researchers formally described the plant as Victoria colombiana last month.“Now that we know this waterlily exists, our responsibility is to understand it better and protect it,” Magdalena said. Researchers estimate that only 30 to 50 individuals may exist in the wild, raising concerns about its survival. They are working towards an official assessment for the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List, aiming for a Critically Endangered classification.Harris photographed the plants in Colombia’s Inírida region in 2021, believing they were Victoria amazonica. Magdalena questioned that identification because the location lay outside the genus’s previously known natural range.He examined satellite images of the river and surrounding lakes and located floating pads that warranted further investigation. The search brought together researchers from Kew and Bogotá’s botanical garden, alongside Indigenous community members familiar with the waterways. Kew’s species profilePlanning the expedition took nearly two years. During five days in the region, the team initially found plants without flowers, which were needed to distinguish the species.On the final night, they departed by boat at 1 am and reached a small lake before sunrise. There they found five plants, including one in flower. They documented seven individuals across two lakes.Nilo Rodríguez, Jaime Hernández and Gustavo Melo helped organise and guide the search. Their knowledge of the region was central to locating the plants.The estimated population is small, but its full extent remains uncertain. Further surveys could reveal additional plants, making the 30-to-50 figure an estimate rather than a confirmed total.Conservation proposals include collecting seeds for cultivation at Bogotá’s botanical garden and establishing a population in a more accessible lake within Indigenous territory. That could support protection, research and community ecotourism. Bogotá city governmentVictoria colombiana adds four known species to the genus. Its predecessor, Victoria boliviana, was identified in 2022 after Kew’s collections had misidentified specimens for 177 years. That earlier discovery was the first new giant waterlily species recognised in more than a century. Kew’s Bolivian waterlily profile
Article Summary: Pictures posted by US plant nursery owner Jeremiah Harris on the Meta-owned social media platform caught the attention of the UK’s Kew waterlily expert Carlos Magdalena. It prompted a search through satellite imagery and an expedition to remote Colombian lakes. Researchers formally described the plant as Victoria colombiana last month.

Article Title: Before Amazon became a global giant, Jeff Bezos and MacKenzie Scott rented a $890-a-month Seattle-area home; 32 years later, Bezos' property portfolio is worth over $700 million
Article Text:
The $890-a-month Bellevue rental where Jeff Bezos started Amazon

Jeff Bezos expanded his Medina estate with a $45 million mansion

New York apartments added to his growing portfolio

Jeff Bezos expanded his Texas ranch to more than 400,000 acres

Beverly Hills purchases included a historic estate

Two Washington mansions became one major project

Hawaii brought a different kind of waterfront property

Miami became his main base after leaving Seattle

From an $890 rental to a portfolio worth more than $700 million

Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available. The Times of India has not independently verified the property details, purchase price, sale price or transaction circumstances mentioned.

Before Amazon became one of the world's largest technology and retail companies, Jeff Bezos and MacKenzie Scott were living in a rented three-bedroom house in Bellevue, Washington, paying just $890 a month, as reported by Architectural Digest. Its garage provided the space where Bezos began working on the online bookshop that launched in 1995. More than three decades later, his property holdings look very different. From waterfront estates and historic Beverly Hills mansions to luxury apartments in New York and a sprawling Texas ranch, Bezos has assembled a real estate portfolio estimated to be worth more than $700 million.In 1994, Bezos and Scott left New York City and settled in Bellevue, Washington. Bezos had been working in finance but decided to pursue an opportunity in the rapidly developing internet market. Reportedly, the couple chose a three-bedroom property measuring around 1,540 square feet, paying $890 each month to live there.Its garage provided space for Bezos to begin working on the online bookshop that would become Amazon. Rather than immediately renting a commercial office, he used the available space to get the business moving.Amazon officially launched in July 1995, although its operations soon outgrew the original arrangement and shifted to larger office and warehouse facilities.Bezos's property purchases began to change as Amazon expanded. In 1998, four years after arriving in Washington state, he spent $10 million on two neighbouring residences in Medina, an affluent community overlooking Lake Washington.The waterfront setting included around 310 feet of private shoreline and a boathouse. The neighbourhood was already home to other prominent technology figures, including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates.Bezos later invested heavily in the estate. In 2010, he reportedly spent $28 million renovating the property. During the same year, he acquired another house next door, adding approximately five acres to his holdings. The Tudor-style residence measured around 24,000 square feet and had been listed for $53 million. Reports put the purchase price at approximately $45 million.Bezos began acquiring property on the opposite coast in 1999, when he paid $7.65 million for three apartments at The Century, an Art Deco building on Manhattan's Upper West Side. The three units, covering approximately 4,400 square feet, included a three-storey penthouse and two apartments immediately below it. Their position offered views across Central Park. In 2012, Bezos reportedly added another 1,725-square-foot apartment in the same building for $5.3 million.His New York holdings expanded considerably in 2019. That year, he bought three apartments overlooking Madison Square Park for a combined $80 million. The purchase included a penthouse spread across three floors, measuring approximately 10,000 square feet, alongside two adjoining residences. The penthouse was designed on a scale that went well beyond a conventional city apartment. It included a ballroom, a library with a marble and glass fireplace, a large main suite and a private observatory, according to reports.Two further purchases followed. Bezos paid $16 million for another three-bedroom apartment in the building in April 2020, then acquired an additional unit for $23 million less than a year later. These transactions brought the reported value of his holdings in the building to $119 million, covering approximately 24,551 square feet.Not all of Bezos's property purchases have been intended as conventional homes. In 2004, he acquired Figure 2 Ranch, a large property near Van Horn in West Texas. The original purchase price has not been publicly established, but the land initially covered around 30,000 acres.The property had previously belonged to attorney Ronald Stasny, who had spent considerable money updating its main residence. Built during the 1920s, the single-storey house underwent changes to its kitchen, bathroom, flooring and porches before Bezos acquired it.The ranch later became known as Corn Ranch and took on a different purpose. It serves as an operational base for Blue Origin, the private aerospace company Bezos established in 2000. Its location and extensive land area made it suitable for the company's work, giving the property a role beyond private residential use.The ranch also has a personal connection for Bezos. He reportedly associated the landscape with memories of visiting his grandfather's ranch in Cotulla, Texas, during his childhood.By 2023, the property had reportedly expanded to more than 400,000 acres. A feature in Vogue, which included a helicopter tour with Lauren Sánchez, offered a look at some of its unusual additions. These included a structure associated with a 10,000-Year Clock, built approximately 500 feet underground, and a bar called the Kármán Line Bar, decorated with space-related memorabilia.A two-storey main residence, swimming pool and several ranch buildings also form part of the property. The scale of Corn Ranch makes it quite different from Bezos's urban apartments and waterfront homes.California became another important part of Bezos's property collection. In 2007, he paid $24.45 million for a Spanish-style residence in Beverly Hills. The property included a main house of nearly 12,000 square feet and a separate guesthouse.The estate had seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms, alongside a greenhouse, swimming pool, formal gardens and a sunken tennis court. Its other features included a six-car garage, a game room and an indoor-outdoor bar.Ten years later, Bezos bought the neighbouring property for $12.9 million. The 1956-built house covered approximately 4,600 square feet and contained four bedrooms. He retained both residences.His largest Beverly Hills purchase came in February 2020. Bezos paid $165 million for the historic Warner estate, previously owned by entertainment businessman David Geffen. The property had originally been designed by architect Roland Coate in 1923 for Harry Warner, one of the founders of Warner Bros. Studios. Set across approximately 10 acres, the estate includes a Georgian-style main house measuring around 13,600 square feet, two guesthouses, a tennis court, a swimming pool and a nine-hole golf course. A large motor court and service garage are also part of the grounds.The main residence has several historic details, including antique wooden flooring reportedly imported from overseas. Bezos followed the purchase with another $10 million acquisition in July 2020, buying the neighbouring 4,615-square-foot property.Renovation work continued over the following years. Aerial photographs published in December 2025 showed additions including pickleball courts, a firepit and a beach volleyball court. Images also revealed a metallic structure resembling a spacecraft capsule, while the swimming pool had undergone changes of its own.Bezos also established a significant presence in the US capital. In late 2016, he spent $23 million on two adjoining mansions in Washington, DC, with a combined floor area of approximately 27,000 square feet.The Georgian-style buildings date back to 1914 and had previously housed the Textile Museum. Their size made them among the largest residential properties in the city. Bezos reportedly intended to combine the two structures into a single family residence.Plans for the renovation included a reported $12 million investment in 2018, with proposals for a garden room among the changes. The combined property was described as having 10 bedrooms and 11 bathrooms.In 2020, Bezos purchased another house across the street for approximately $5 million. The additional property provided further separation from the surrounding neighbourhood while adding to his Washington holdings.One of Bezos's other major purchases in 2020 took him to Maui, Hawaii. He acquired a compound near La Perouse Bay, reportedly valued at around $78 million. At the time, the transaction was described as a record for the island's most expensive residential property sale.The arrangement was unusual because Bezos bought the company holding the land rather than purchasing the property directly. The site covers approximately 14 acres and includes a main residence measuring 4,500 square feet, with three bedrooms and three bathrooms.Two guesthouses provide additional accommodation, while an outdoor kitchen and a 700-square-foot swimming pool overlook the surrounding coastal landscape. The property also includes access to a two-acre deeded cove.Its position beside the Pacific Ocean and private beach distinguishes it from the urban residences in his collection. The Hawaiian compound remains another example of how widely Bezos's property interests have spread.Bezos's move towards Florida became public in late 2023, when he announced plans to relocate from Seattle to Miami. The decision coincided with a series of purchases on Indian Creek Island, a privately developed barrier island known for its concentration of wealthy residents.The location is often called Billionaire Bunker. Among its high-profile property owners are Mark Zuckerberg, Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, Tom Brady and David Guetta.Bezos began building his presence there in August 2023, paying $68 million for a waterfront estate covering approximately 2.8 acres. The existing residence, originally constructed in 1965, measured around 9,300 square feet and contained three bedrooms and three bathrooms.Just two months later, he acquired the neighbouring Mediterranean-style mansion for another $79 million. At approximately 19,000 square feet, it was considerably larger, with seven bedrooms and 14 bathrooms. A third purchase followed in April 2024. Bezos paid $90 million for another residence on the island, bringing his reported spending on Indian Creek properties to $237 million. The third house covers around 12,000 square feet and has six bedrooms and nine bathrooms.The distance between Bezos's first Bellevue rental and his current property collection is considerable. The $890 monthly home was a three-bedroom house where a garage provided the working space for a new online business. His later purchases include historic estates, large city apartments, private waterfront compounds and thousands of acres of Texas land.His move to Miami has changed where he spends much of his time, but it has not meant abandoning every earlier property. He continues to maintain holdings in several locations, including Seattle, California, Washington, DC, New York, Texas and Hawaii.The estimated value of his real estate portfolio now exceeds $700 million. That figure sits alongside a business career that began with an online bookshop launched in 1995 and developed into one of the world's largest technology and retail companies.

What happened at the crossing

Article Title: Former SpaceX engineers launched startup in 2024 to make device that turns seawater into drinking water
Article Text:
How the $749 desalination device works

Making desalination affordable and simple

Former SpaceX engineers are offering a backup plan when a disaster knocks out a city’s water supply. In such cases, a few extra cases of bottled water in the pantry won't last very long. Vital Lyfe, a startup launched in 2024, is working on a portable desalination device that can quickly turn almost any nearby natural water source, including seawater, into safe drinking water. Called Access, the $749 machine is roughly the size of a large toolbox, and it is designed for anyone needing reliable off-grid water, from campers and sailors to communities without steady access to clean drinking water.Using the device is straightforward. A user drops a hose into a water source and pushes a button. Inside, a battery-powered, high-pressure pump forces the water through a reverse osmosis membrane, filtering out salt and other impurities. Access can process up to 6 gallons (around 22.7 liters) of seawater per hour, or up to 12 gallons (around 45.4 litres) of fresh water per hour.It also fixes one of the biggest headaches of existing portable units: maintenance. Changing the filters on Access takes less than 30 seconds. When Vital Lyfe’s founders tested competing products on the market, it took them – as experienced engineers – 30 to 60 minutes just to swap out a filter.Traditional desalination usually requires massive infrastructure, such as a sprawling 6-acre plant in San Diego. Smaller, portable desalination systems, often called marine “watermakers”, already exist, but they are difficult to maintain and typically cost thousands of dollars.“Developing nations have essentially been priced out of this technology,” Fast Company quoted Jonathan Criss, CEO and cofounder of Vital Lyfe.To bring the price down, the founders started with standard reverse osmosis and stripped the system down using first-principles engineering. They re-evaluated every single part, cutting out unnecessary components to lower costs and make repairs simple.They also built the product specifically for mass production. “We always say that we design the manufacturing line before the product,” Criss added.Vital Lyfe’s factory, located near SpaceX’s plant in the Los Angeles area, is built for high-speed output. “In theory, based off of what we’ve designed this factory for, you can build more deSal devices over the course of a month here than currently exist globally,” Criss added.Right now, Vital Lyfe is targeting recreational users, campers and emergency preppers. At the same time, the company is partnering with nonprofits to get the units into regions facing severe water shortages, expecting the $749 price tag to drop further as production scales up.
Article Summary: Vital Lyfe, a startup launched in 2024, is working on a portable desalination device. Called Access, the $749 machine is roughly the size of a large toolbox. It is designed for anyone needing reliable off-grid water, from campers and sailors to communities without steady access to clean drinking water. Changing the filters on Access takes less than 30 seconds.

Article Title: Anthropic may be the first casualty of US midterm elections, investors see IPO valuation drop from $2 trillion to ….
Article Text:
Anthropic

Wall Street turn cold on AI

Voters push back against data centers and tech power

Anthropic steps into the spotlight

American voters made their frustration with tech billionaires and artificial intelligence (AI) clear at the ballot box this week. Now, Anthropic is walking straight into that headwind as it prepares to go public. According to a report, the AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic Nasdaq debut, likely aiming for mid-November. According to a CNBC report, Anthropic investors expect the company to target a valuation between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion, which is essentially a noticeable step down from the $2 trillion figure floated in recent months.From Wall Street to Main Street, the backdrop for Anthropic’s public offering has grown much tougher. Last week, the Nasdaq logged its steepest drop in 19 months. The index is already down to start November, following an October that stood as its worst month since March 2025. Companies tied most closely to the AI infrastructure buildout, particularly chipmakers and neocloud providers, are taking the hardest hit in the selloff.On November 3, voters delivered a sharp rebuke to the AI sector while handing Democrats sweeping congressional victories nationwide.Candidates who campaigned on stricter AI regulations won easily in Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia – all of which will now have Democratic governors.Local resistance was just as stark: communities voted down data centre-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 races. According to an NBC News exit poll, more than half of voters said AI data centers were a “crucial” or “major factor” in choosing who to back for Congress.“People don’t want a data center going near them if it’s just going to house AI that’s going to help a big tech company profit. What Anthropic is doing when they’re going public with such a high valuation is they’re really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that’s not going to go well with the public,” CNBC quoted Maura Austin, a behavioural scientist at the University of Virginia, as saying.Founded by CEO Dario Amodei and a group of researchers who broke away from OpenAI, Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI’s risks and benefits seriously. It is best known for building the Claude family of AI models, which it sells mostly to other businesses. Due to that corporate focus, Anthropic largely avoided becoming the public face of AI, leaving that spotlight to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman.

According to a CNBC report, Anthropic investors expect the company to target a valuation between $1 trillion and $1.5 trillion. The Nasdaq logged its steepest drop in 19 months last week.

Article Title: California shuts door on the billionaire wealth tax for which Google co-founder Sergey Brin spent millions but voters in two ‘AI capitals’ wanted it
Article Text:
Google co-founder Sergey Brin

Silicon Valley splits over the 5% tax

Sergey Brin’s $102 million push and a competing ban

California’s high-stakes, controversial billionaire wealth tax proposal is defeated. Statewide, voters are rejecting Proposition 40 by a 55% to 45% margin. The outcome delivers a major victory to Silicon Valley’s wealthiest residents, including Sergey Brin , and business interests, who poured hundreds of millions of dollars into stopping the measure – even as voters in two of the state’s biggest cities backed it.Prop 40 sought to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of roughly 200 California billionaires. Backed primarily by the state’s powerful healthcare workers' union, the measure was designed to raise money for healthcare and help offset Medi-Cal cuts for low-income residents. In the heart of Silicon Valley, voters overwhelmingly sided against it. Santa Clara County, home to tech hubs like Sunnyvale, Palo Alto, Cupertino and Mountain View, mirrored the state’s 55% “no” to 45% “yes” split. Wealthy Bay Area neighbours in Marin County to the north and San Mateo County to the south also voted it down.Yet the results revealed a striking divide inside California's tech and AI corridors. In San Francisco County, 55% of voters backed Prop 40 while 45% opposed it. That support came despite the city serving as headquarters for major AI startups like OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are preparing to go public and mint a fresh wave of millionaires and billionaires.Meanwhile, Los Angeles County also voted in favour of Prop 40, passing it 53% to 47%. Unlike Northern California’s tech-driven economy, Southern California’s entertainment industry largely views AI-generated content as a threat rather than a windfall.No single person spent more to defeat the wealth tax than Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who contributed $102 million to the campaign. Overall, billionaire opponents and business groups spent $316.7 million to fight Prop 40.To make sure the tax couldn't sneak through, opponents also placed two competing countermeasures on the ballot: Propositions 41 and 42. One of them, Prop 42, is currently leading in the vote count. By prohibiting taxes on personal savings, assets, and retirement holdings, Prop 42 would effectively ban wealth taxes in California altogether.While Brin and his fellow California billionaires appear to have won this round at the state level, the broader fight over taxing the ultra-wealthy isn't over. Now Democrats control Congress in Washington, and lawmakers are picking up efforts to make billionaires pay more taxes, which could mean more pressure on rich Americans at the federal level.
Article Summary: Prop 40 sought to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of roughly 200 California billionaires. Backed primarily by the state’s powerful healthcare workers' union, the measure was designed to raise money for healthcare and help offset Medi-Cal cuts for low-income residents. In the heart of Silicon Valley, voters overwhelmingly sided against it.

Article Title: As Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees, staff write open letter; says: Working at Microsoft has become joyless and...
Article Text:
FILE - The logo of Microsoft is seen outside its French headquarters in Issy-les-Moulineaux, outside Paris on May 13, 2024. (AP Photo/Thibault Camus, File)

Microsoft employees say mandatory AI tools are making their work worse

Microsoft buyout covers employees in India, US, UK and Canada

Microsoft's record profits and AI spending sit beside raises below 1%

A group of current and former Microsoft employees is circulating an open letter accusing the company of chasing artificial intelligence at the cost of its own people, customers and climate goals. The letter has drawn fresh attention after Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its workforce. It is the largest such offer in the company’s history.Signed “Concerned Microsoft Workers,” the letter says that for many staff, “working at Microsoft has become joyless and demoralizing.” It ties the slump in morale to the period when the company ramped up its AI investments. It also points to heavy workloads, constant reorganisations and the threat of being replaced by AI.According to a report by The New York Times, the letter began doing the rounds among colleagues before the October 26 buyout announcement. It asks Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how AI is built and used, and to stop linking AI use to rewards or reprimands.The letter is blunt about what AI adoption looks like on the ground. Workers say they are pushed to use AI tools in almost every part of their jobs, often with little or no training and no reason given beyond speed.The result, they write, is a costly cycle of learning new tools, cleaning up poor AI output and rolling back weak features.The complaints go beyond the office. The signatories claim the company’s own research shows AI agents do not put user safety first, and that internal planning documents describe ways to get people hooked on AI products. They also object to secretive data centre projects, contracts with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Israeli military, and what they call circular investments among a handful of AI firms.Their demands fall under three headings: no AI without worker input and protections, no AI without community protections, and no trading away environmental promises for AI. On the last point, they want Microsoft to recommit to being carbon negative, water positive and zero waste by 2030. The group is open to full-time staff, employees of subsidiaries like GitHub and LinkedIn, vendors, interns and contractors.The Voluntary Exit Offer went to eligible employees at level 70 and below in participating teams across India, the US, the UK and Canada. Sales and some engineering teams were left out. Those who accept get at least eight weeks of base pay, with the amount rising by level and tenure. They have until December 9 to decide and would leave on December 31.In a note to staff, chief people officer Amy Coleman called it “a new choice to make that transition now with support.” The company expects fewer than 5% of eligible employees to sign up.This is Microsoft’s second buyout of 2026. In April, about 8,600 long-serving US employees were offered early retirement, and roughly 30% took it. In July, the company cut about 4,800 jobs, including a fifth of its Xbox workforce. That followed 10,000 layoffs in 2023 and more than 15,000 in 2025. Headcount stood at 223,000 in June, down 5,000 from a year earlier.The timing has not gone unnoticed inside the company. Two days after the buyouts were announced, Microsoft reported quarterly profit of $36.6 billion, up 32%, on revenue of $92.3 billion. Capital spending, mostly on data centres, rose 30% to $45.2 billion. The company expects to spend about $170 billion this calendar year.Employees told The New York Times that merit raises this year were unusually small, in some cases under 1%. At a town hall last month, a question on how leadership balanced over $100 billion a year in AI spending against flat rewards drew more than 80 reactions, about double what most questions got.Gretchen Thomas, a 57-year-old design leader who left in September after five years, told the publication her stock award was cut partly for not consistently showing speed and a willingness to experiment, including with AI. “I just can’t believe how grim it’s gotten just in the last three years,” she said.Coleman has said the buyouts are not linked to how AI is changing work, the report noted. She did not rule out future layoffs either.For those who stay, the bigger worry is the work left behind. Several employees said they do not expect departing colleagues to be replaced, which leaves more on their plates as the AI push carries on.
Article Summary: Microsoft buyout covers employees in India, US, UK and Canada. Workers say they are pushed to use AI tools in almost every part of their jobs, often with little or no training and no reason given beyond speed. Microsoft's record profits and AI spending sit beside raises below 1% in some cases.

Article Title: Tesla to 'end' Cybertruck, a truck Elon Musk once called Tesla's best product ever; Musk says: Winding down production at Gigafactory Texas to make room for...
Article Text:
Musk’s “best product ever” is ending

Cybertruck sales fell far short of Musk's 250,000-a-year target

Tesla's Texas Gigafactory shifts to Cybercab and Optimus robot production

Tesla will stop building the Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas around the middle of 2027, CEO Elon Musk has announced. In a post on X on Friday, Musk said the company would be "winding down production" of the stainless-steel pickup to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis. Musk did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere. Texas is the only plant that makes it, and its steel body needs specialised tooling, so shifting production would not come cheap. Wes Morrill, the project's lead engineer, hinted at a full stop, writing on X that the Cybertruck "lives on through Cybercab."When a fan called it the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, Musk replied, "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time." He has made that claim himself, calling it Tesla's best product ever on a 2019 earnings call and again in April this year. Tesla shares rose over 4% on Friday.Musk once expected the Cybertruck to sell 250,000 units a year, and by late 2023 he claimed more than a million reservations. Very few of those turned into sales. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 20,237 in the US in 2025, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. In October 2026, just 1,914 were registered in the US, according to Motor Intelligence.Ford sold over 70,000 F-Series trucks that month.Tesla does not report Cybertruck numbers separately, but its "other models" category, which includes the truck, managed only 8,300 deliveries in the third quarter. One of the biggest buyers last year was Musk's own SpaceX, which spent $131 million on Cybertrucks at full retail price, as per a company filing.The trouble started early. At the 2019 unveiling, Tesla's design chief threw a metal ball at the truck's supposedly armoured window, and it cracked on stage. Deliveries began only in late 2023, after years of delays. The truck was first promised at $39,900, but the base model arrived at about $61,000, and the top Cyberbeast trim now costs $102,000. Even before deliveries began, Musk admitted on a 2023 earnings call, "We dug our own grave with Cybertruck. "Recalls followed. The 2024 model alone faced 11 voluntary recalls in the US, including one over an accelerator pedal that could get stuck. Another in 2025 covered more than 46,000 trucks over a trim panel that could fall off. The Cybertruck never went on sale in Europe either, as it failed to meet safety standards there.The Texas factory will now focus on the Cybercab, a two-seater with no steering wheel that already offers paid rides in parts of Austin. It will also build Tesla's Optimus humanoid robot.The exit leaves Tesla with its smallest lineup in over a decade, after the Model S and Model X were dropped earlier this year. The Model 3 and Model Y now carry its car business, accounting for 478,000 deliveries in the third quarter.The news capped a rough week for Musk, after Republican candidates he backed with around $446 million lost in the US midterms.
Article Summary: Cybertruck sales fell far short of Musk's 250,000-a-year target. Texas factory will now focus on the Cybercab, a two-seater with no steering wheel that already offers paid rides in parts of Austin. Tesla shares rose over 4% on Friday.

Article Title: Meta president Dina Powell McCormick on new US governors: Not all are against data centres; one told her: As soon as we get past the inauguration, let's...
Article Text:
Dina Powell McCormick, Meta president and vice chair, speaks during an interview with Maria Bartiromo on the FOX Business Network's Mornings with Maria show, Tuesday, June 9, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)

Meta expects tougher scrutiny for new data centres after the US midterms

Big tech is now weighing AI data centres outside the US

Meta president Dina Powell McCormick expects the US midterm results to make data centres harder to build. She also thinks some of the politicians who campaigned against them may be more willing to talk than their speeches suggest. Powell McCormick spoke with WSJ editor-in-chief Emma Tucker at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa on Wednesday. She said one governor who won on Tuesday, after making data centres a major campaign issue, contacted Meta soon after. "As soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet," the governor told her. They said they did not want to lose the investment, adding, "We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere."She did not name the governor.Her comments came a day after Democrats won statehouses in Texas, Georgia, Ohio and Michigan, all key states for data centre sites. According to WSJ, opposition to the facilities featured heavily in campaign ads and exit polls. The incoming governors of Ohio and Texas have both called for conditional freezes on new construction. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to halt new projects until protections for residents are in place.The friendly call aside, Powell McCormick was clear that the road ahead looks tougher. She expects "a lot more review" of new projects and said starting fresh build-outs in the US will be "very challenging."Expanding existing sites is a different matter. Communities that have hosted Meta's facilities for a few years have felt the benefits rather than the costs, she argued. Meta has data centres in 23 states, and five of them are planned at 1 gigawatt or more.She said Meta has a working formula for local support. The company pays for its own electricity, directs tax surpluses towards teachers and first responders, hires locally and seeks backing from both parties.The industry, she admitted, has not explained its case well enough. Her answer is for tech companies to talk far more about what data centres offer the towns around them.Powell McCormick, who said she spends about 80% of her time securing computing power, added that every hyperscaler is now asking whether it needs to build outside the US. Given the size of these investments, she called hedging them a wise move.The stakes are high for Meta. The company is racing to build enough computing power to run Muse, its personal AI agents, for its 3.6 billion users. It plans to spend up to $145 billion in capital expenditure this year, WSJ reported. Its biggest projects include Hyperion in Louisiana, Prometheus in Ohio and a third site in Texas being built with BlackRock. Two of those three now sit in states with incoming governors who favour a pause.Even if Muse grows slower than hoped, Powell McCormick said Meta gets calls every day from companies wanting to lease the compute it has built.Meta is not the only one reworking its plans. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged public concerns over water use during an internal Q&A and floated the idea of building in the desert, according to WSJ. OpenAI has since pledged not to make public officials sign nondisclosure agreements during data centre talks. Investor Brad Gerstner estimates that up to 35% of US data centre construction planned for next year could be at risk. Anthropic, in its IPO filing, warned investors that local moratoriums could delay or block the facilities it depends on for compute.For now, Meta is betting that the governor who called will not be the only one ready to sit down once the inauguration is over.
Article Summary: Meta president Dina Powell McCormick expects tougher scrutiny for new data centres after the US midterms. She thinks some of the politicians who campaigned against them may be more willing to talk than their speeches suggest. Every hyperscaler is now asking whether it needs to build outside the US, she said.

Article Title: US government memo said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang; she is believed to be a spy recruited by Chinese ministry; lawmakers now have questions on...
Article Text:
US memo links Jensen Huang to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang

Megaspeed bought billions in Nvidia hardware while Alice Huang was a top executive

Three House committees want Jensen Huang to explain his Megaspeed ties on November 18

US security officials are frustrated by Huang’s lobbying for China chip sales

US officials believe Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who American intelligence thinks was recruited to spy for China, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter.The claim comes from a government memo written earlier this year using information gathered by US intelligence. According to the FT, it was shared with a small group of top officials shortly before President Donald Trump travelled to Beijing for his May summit with Xi Jinping . Alice Huang is believed to have been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, the country’s main spy agency.Nvidia declined to comment on the memo or the claim of an intimate relationship. The company has previously said Huang meets “thousands of customer executives every year.” The White House and the CIA also declined to comment, and Alice Huang could not be reached. Neither she nor Megaspeed has been charged with a crime. The two Huangs are not related.Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen. She was listed as Megaspeed’s managing director for its first eight months and has described herself as its CEO, though she has since left.The company was spun off in 2023 from 7Road, a Chinese gaming and cloud firm partly owned by the Chinese government.Washington has been watching Megaspeed since late 2024. That year, a Commerce Department official visited its Malaysian data centre and found Nvidia equipment still packed in boxes, which suggested the hardware was passing through rather than being installed. The New York Times, citing trade records, reported that Megaspeed’s Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced AI equipment with Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026.Nvidia says its own checks found no evidence of chips being diverted to China.The two executives have been photographed together more than once: at a Taipei bar with a group of customers around Computex in June 2024, and leaving a Taipei restaurant after a business dinner in May 2025.The FT report landed a day after three Republican chairmen asked Huang to sit for a joint, closed-door briefing. Brian Mast of the Foreign Affairs Committee, John Moolenaar of the Select Committee on China and Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee want him to discuss his interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s safeguards against foreign espionage.“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote.The request is voluntary, not a subpoena. It follows a New York Times report last month that US spy agencies learned of the relationship by surveilling Alice Huang. Huang has described his dealings with her as normal business and said the US government never told him about its suspicions.It also marks a shift for Republican leaders, who have mostly followed Trump’s hands-off line on tech. Anti-tech sentiment largely helped Democrats in the midterms, and Senator Elizabeth Warren has renewed her call for Huang to testify.The allegations land on a CEO with rare access to the White House. National security officials have privately voiced frustration with Huang, who personally lobbied Trump this year to let Nvidia sell its H200 chip to Chinese customers, the FT reported.Huang has met Trump several times since his second term began. When Trump left for Beijing in May, Huang was not among the CEOs on Air Force One. Trump called him after learning this, and Huang flew to Alaska to board the presidential jet during a stopover. In September, he attended Trump’s state dinner for Xi.The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Beijing has previously called claims that it was spying on Nvidia groundless.So far, the memo has reached Capitol Hill only through press reports. Huang has until Wednesday, November 11, to tell lawmakers whether he will answer questions about it in person.
Article Summary: Three House committees want Jensen Huang to explain his Megaspeed ties on November 18. US security officials are frustrated by Huang’s lobbying for China chip sales.Megaspeed bought billions in Nvidia hardware while Alice Huang was a top executive.

Article Title: As Oracle makes a 'will not do' pledge to worried investors; analysts say company is trying to show that there's a method to the madness in ...
Article Text:
As Oracle makes a 'will not do' pledge to worried investors; analysts say company is trying to show that there's a method to the madness in ..

Oracle becomes a concern for investors

Oracle to cut back on outside financing

Last month, Oracle told its investors that it will not raise more than $20 billion in additional financing for AI through fiscal 2030. According to a Reuters report then, the pledge is meant to reassure worried investors that the company led by Larry Ellison will need ever-larger ‌sums of outside money to fund its aggressive data-center buildout. Speaking at the company’s investor day in Las Vegas, CFO Hilary Maxson said Oracle also expects free cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. It is expected to top $30 billion in fiscal 2029, as the capital spending declines. Following the announcement, Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne, as quoted in Reuters report, said: “Oracle is trying to show investors that there's a method to the madness of its massive AI infrastructure spending”."Though ⁠the projections are ambitious and far from guaranteed, they demonstrate an understanding of investors' concerns and offer an optimistic path toward ​addressing them."As stated in the report, Oracle has become a major concern in the AI industry because it does not have the large and steady revenue streams of cloud giants such as Microsoft and Amazon. It also depends heavily on OpenAI , the ChatGPT maker that is still losing money.The deal with OpenAI has added hundreds of billions of dollars in future cloud business to Oracle’s order book. However, building the data centres and other infrastructure needed to meet these commitments has pushed Oracle to rely heavily on borrowing money and selling shares.In October, Oracle said it plans to reduce its initial spending by using vendor financing, hardware provided by customers and advance payments from customers. These steps are expected to help the company manage its cash needs until it starts generating positive free cash flow. The company also expects to stop depending on external funding for its growth from fiscal 2029. It also forecasts that its net debt will fall to less than 3.5 times its annual core earnings that year.Earlier this year, Oracle said it planned to raise $40 billion through debt and stock sales during the current financial year. This included a $20 billion stock sale that it completed in the first quarter. As of August 31, Oracle had $125.34 billion in debt and other borrowings, while its cash and cash equivalents stood at around $36.37 billion."I've told you we ​need an additional up ⁠to $20 billion in funding for the remainder of our fiscal 2027," Maxson said."We're announcing that this $20 billion, split evenly between debt and equity, is the final amount needed to fund the remainder of ​this cycle."
Article Summary: Oracle has become a major concern in the AI industry because it does not have the large and steady revenue streams of cloud giants such as Microsoft and Amazon. It also depends heavily on OpenAI, the ChatGPT maker that is still losing money. The company expects to stop depending on external funding for its growth from fiscal 2029.

Article Title: America's Delaware state's proposal to run AI Agents run companies and not human CEOs, to be investigated, Governor Matt Meyer gets 'complaint letter' asking how ...
Article Text:
A representative picture.

Dear Governor Meyer:

James Comer, Chairman, Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

Delaware state's proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents is facing protest. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) is investigating the State of Delaware’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC). Under the proposal, an AI Agent would an AI agent would run day-to-day operations of a corporate entity while providing the human or entity behind the AIC with liability protections from potential harms to consumers, the public, and business partners perpetuated by the controlling AI.In a letter to Delaware Governor Matt Meyer, Chairman Comer requests documents and information on the state’s assessed risks of this initiative, as well as the forces driving Delaware and other states to adopt such proposals. Read the letter:The Committee on Oversight and Government Reform seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC). According to your Secretary of State, an AIC would be run day-to-day by an artificial intelligence (AI) agent while providing the human or entity capitalizing the AIC with liability protections from potential harms to business partners, consumers, and the public, perpetrated by the controlling AI “except where [the capitalizer] fails to capitalize the company or uses it to commit fraud or a willful violation of law.While this Committee has promoted2 the importance and potential of AI technologies to benefit U.S. citizens, the work of governments, and the global economy, it has also conducted oversight examining uses of artificial intelligence that may be harmful, unfair, or non-transparent to consumers or other businesses through surveillance pricing, assessment of housing fees, and for rental car damage billing. We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives.On July 23, 2025, you signed Delaware House Joint Resolution, which directed Delaware’s Artificial Intelligence Commission to work with your appointed Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez to create “a regulatory sandbox framework for the testing of innovative and novel technologies that utilize agentic artificial intelligence.” The resolution directed the state AI Commission, in collaboration with the Secretary of State, to deliver a written report of findings and recommendations no later than January 2, 2026. The subsequent report of the Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission addressed to you and other state officials on December 22, 2025, noted that a Commission subcommittee is “actively working towards a draft regulatory framework that would create a regulatory sandbox that would test and evaluate agentic artificial intelligence and its application to corporate governance.”7 The twopage report referencing House Joint Resolution 7 did not mention any commission efforts to assess the potential safety, harms, risks, or outside consultations with independent experts associated with the proposal.In late June 2026, authors released a draft 36-page legislative proposal that is reportedly “likely to be introduced in the General Assembly next year.”9 John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer whose biography at Delaware based firm Richards, Layton, & Finger describes him as having represented Facebook (now Meta) and other clients focused on “complex transactional matters involving Delaware corporations, including mergers and acquisitions, corporate governance, and corporate finance” is described as the “principal drafter of the proposed legislation. ” According to Zeberkiewicz, “Anything that a company can do, the AIC can do as a company.”He further specified this would include allowing AI agents to engage in just about any business activity from providing coding services to filing lawsuits and would protect owners of new AICs fromfacing legal liability from actions the AI might take.13 Delaware Secretary of State PatibandaSanchez, in a joint op-ed with an AI company CEO contributing to the project wrote, “Delaware sees this and intends to set the norms for governing AI agents. The legal system has admitted new kinds of actors before. The stakes are higher now, and the timeline shorter with AI capabilities rapidly advancing. We invite the companies building agentic systems to develop the AIC framework with us. ”14 Patibanda-Sanchez was also quoted the same month on the importance of the proposal for positioning Delaware as a haven for registering companies, “Should a new entity form be created out of it, that’s a really huge benefit to our state’s revenues.”One Delaware media outlet reporting on the proposal noted, “It is not immediately clear whether any large company or lobbying group asked Delaware to propose its AI testing ground.”16 In September 2026, a different media outlet noted the Delaware Secretary of State’s office declined to answer questions about the nature of the state’s working relationship with an AI company contributing to the proposal.While Delaware officials tout the benefits of an AIC regulatory framework for creating transparency around the decision making of an agentic AI, such transparency does not appear to exist in this policy making initiative that may soon result in new state law. The Committee seeks information regarding how Delaware has considered the risks of this initiative as well as the forces driving Delaware, and possibly other states, to adopt such proposals to inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives.To assist the Committee’s oversight of this matter, we request the following information, covering the time period January 1, 2025, to the present, unless otherwise indicated, as soon as possible but no later than November 9, 2026:1. All documents and communications, including those to or from non-government entities or persons, including internal AI chat logs, held by your administration regarding policy development efforts or inputs for AIC and any other discussion about artificial intelligence and liability;2. All ethics, consulting, and other agreements completed by contributors from outside government to AIC policy development;3. All documents and communications, including those with all individuals or entities consulted, regarding possible safety concerns and harms related to AIC and efforts to limit liability for artificial intelligence;4. All drafts and all comments and inputs provided for all AIC policy proposals and proposal outlines considered by state officials. The Committee on Oversight and Government Reform is the principal oversight committee of the U.S. House of Representatives and has broad authority to investigate “any matter” at “any time” under House Rule X.18 House Rule X also provides the Committee jurisdiction to study intergovernmental relationships including those of states. To arrange for the delivery of documents, or if you have any questions, please contact Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Majority staff at (202) 225-5074.
Article Summary: Delaware state's proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents is facing protest. House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Chairman James Comer (R-Ky.) is investigating the State of Delaware’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC)

Article Title: When Jeff Bezos on stage shared what world's biggest investor Warren Buffet said when he asked him why people don't 'exactly copy' his investment strategy
Article Text:
When Jeff Bezos on stage shared what world's biggest investor Warren Buffet said when he asked him why people don't 'exactly copy' his investment strategy

What Warren Buffett told Jeff Bezos about his investment strategy

Jeff Bezos also built Amazon with a long-term approach

Getting rich through investing is a goal many people share, but building wealth over decades requires patience. While some investors look for quick returns, Warren Buffett has long followed a strategy built around long-term investments and the power of compounding. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos once asked Warren Buffett why more people did not follow his investment approach, despite its simplicity. Buffett’s response, shared by Bezos at the America Business Forum in Miami in 2025, highlighted a key reason why many investors struggle to stay focused on long-term gains.“I once asked Warren Buffett, why don’t more people copy your investment strategy?” Jeff Bezos said on stage at the America Business Forum in Miami in 2025. “It’s not that difficult to understand in principle. And he said, ‘Oh, Jeff, that’s easy. My approach is a get-rich-slowly scheme.'”Jeff Bezos then explained why Buffett’s approach may be difficult for many people to follow.“And people don’t like those,” he continued. “But there’s a lot of truth in that for everything, which is if you can think in terms of seven years instead of three years, and you can defer gratification and think long term, that will give you a head start against all of your competitors because most people can’t do that.”Warren Buffett’s investment strategy has focused on buying strong businesses at reasonable prices and holding them for long periods. He has often stressed the importance of patience rather than trying to predict short-term market movements.In his 1988 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, Buffett wrote, “Our favorite holding period is forever.” The approach relies on allowing investments to grow over time. Compounding can have a greater effect over longer periods, although investment returns are never guaranteed.Bezos has also spoken about the importance of thinking beyond short-term results. Amazon’s first shareholder letter in 1997 carried the heading “It’s All About the Long Term.”The company invested heavily in warehouses, technology and new businesses during its early years. Amazon reported its first full-year profit in 2003, six years after the letter was published.Bezos’ remarks in Miami reflected the same principle: focusing on a longer time horizon can offer an advantage when others are prioritising quicker results.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos once asked Warren Buffett why more people did not follow his investment approach, despite its simplicity. Buffett’s response highlighted a key reason why many investors struggle to stay focused on long-term gains. Warren Buffett has long followed a strategy built around long- term investments and the power of compounding.

Article Title: Google executive Donald Harrison has resigned from SpaceX board with immediate effect; CEO Elon Musk says: At this point, there are simply too many ...
Article Text:
Elon Musk sends 'let's go to Space' message hours after mid-term election results

Elon Musk's Spacex has announced the departure of its longtime Google executive Donald Harrison. In an SEC filing the company said that Harrison has resigned from the rocket maker’s board of directors. Harrison is an old-timer at Google. He has worked at Google since 2005, and is the search giant’s president of global partnerships and corporate development.
